projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Robert Zito was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mr. Zito served with the US Marine Corps Third Wing, VMF 511. He served in the Pacific Theater and his highest rank was Sergeant. I'm Tom Swope. We recorded this at Mr. Zito's home in Rocky River, Ohio on May 17, 2001. Mr. Zito's age at the time of this recording is 76. . . .

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: I always wanted to be a Marine--That's a story in itself . . . My dad was a barber in Geneva and he had a table in the barbershop and people would wait and they could read. I used to go in--he had a big book yay big (gesturing), with pictures and captions about WWI. And, he served in the Italian Army in the first war. Anyway, it seemed to me that the Marines won the war because every other picture was about the Marines, you know, Marne, and, I can't think of all the French villages that they were involved in, but apparently the Marines were very, very influential in the thing, so being a Marine was important to me, and-- before I went in I would shoot pool (laughter) at a local pool shooting shop and everybody smoked a cigar or cigarette or something--I've got a carrot, you know--I've got to shoot, I put my carrot down on the table because I wanted to make sure my eyes were going to be good enough to qualify and so, you know,-- I don't know what I'd have done,-- I'd have been devastated if I couldn't have gotten in because I really . . . It was important to me, and, why? Just because I wanted to be one of the good guys, you know, not that there's anything wrong with the Army, the Navy and so on. I had the greatest respect for those Merchant Marine guys, they took a beating, you know, anybody involved in the war took a beating of one kind or another--it was a tough time. So, but as far as, you know, you talking to me and so on, I never got a chance to be a hero (laughter) but they worked on us so that when the time came you weren't afraid to do what you had to do, and heroes come in two sizes--dead ones and live ones--and they really, they did a great job on our attitudes and such. Really, one of the best things that ever happened to me was my time in the Marines.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Obviously, you signed up for the Marines?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Yeah, I loved it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When did you go in?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: I went in March of '43 and I had graduated from high school and spent some time in college. I shouldn't say it, but I shouldn't have been there because I would have never thought I'd be a college student because I was already a licensed barber and my dad was a barber, had a barber shop in Geneva, and I figured that was what I was going to do for the rest of my life. And, it so happened that I could play football and I got a football scholarship, so I went to college (laughter) to be honest with you, just to play football. But while I was in the service, and as I said before, it was one of the best things that ever happened to me, it made a big difference, and I leaned that if you didn't have that education you weren't going very far. So, I started--I took courses in algebra and school was never hard for me, it just never was important to me because I didn't need it-- I already had my education for my life's work. Anyway, I took correspondence courses and it was good for me. But anyway, where do you want to go from here?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where did you train?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: I went to San Diego. I was supposed to go to Paris Island but they had an epidemic of spinal meningitis, which was quite common in those days--I guess it still is--so, those of us who were supposed to go to Paris Island ended up in San Diego where they picked up an epidemic (laughter) of spinal meningitis, so it really didn't make much difference, although I would have preferred to go to Paris Island because Paris Island had the reputation of being the Marine Corps training grounds, you know, although basically, San Diego was tough enough.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Would that be Pendleton?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: No, San Diego Naval Air Station, and there was a Marine contingent there and it was 90 days of fun (laughter).

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm Hmm. What do you remember? Any vivid memories of that experience?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Boot camp?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Oh, my. (laughter). How much time do we got?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: A lot. I've got lots of tape!

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: I could go on and on about that. No, it--I got to say, Tom, that I just loved it. I mean, I--there was never a doubt. When the war was over I wanted to go home and never thought about re-upping, you know. My brother, Jim, who was in the Navy, he was an ensign, just died last year, often said "If I had it to do over again I would have stayed in the Navy." He loved the regimentation, he loved the everything in its place, you know, and the camaraderie and so on and so forth, but, you know, some guys did and some guys didn't. Boot camp was a revelation for everybody because you just don't treat people like that (laughter). I mean, they did what they did for a purpose and they weeded out people who had no business being there. Now, they tried to do that in advance with the psychological testing and so on and so forth, but I can remember guys breaking down in tears because they just didn't understand why they were talking to us that way. I mean, we're on their side (laughter), and they could be rough, and they had their ways of punishing the misfits. We had one guy, his name was Lautenschlager, (ph) I can't think of the first name, but he was out of Detroit, and had a bit of a record, and he told us all of this, you know, maybe it was not true, I don't know. But, we were on the rifle range one time and (laughter) he really wasn't--he was a misfit, and this one time he is down on his belly in the prone position, but the barrel of the rifle wasn't level and the drill instructor would give him a bad time about it, and finally he jumped up and he stepped on the barrel to level it out and it hurt; he had that thing tucked up in his shoulder, you know, and Lautenschlager got up and hit him with a rifle (laughter). It was almost funny because that was the way he handled it. To him, it was the thing to do. I mean, some guy did something to him, he needed a whack in the head with a rifle. And, Tyrone Power was in our outfit on the range, not in our platoon, but he was on the range at the same time I was. Very impressive guy. And, he had a tough time, because everything he did there were 20 people standing around him watching: reporters, radio people, no television people (laughter), and he just--he didn't qualify the first time on the range because guys were practically sitting on him while he was trying to zero in and so somebody got the idea that maybe he'd do better if he were left alone and he did fine. Nice, nice guy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you talk to him much?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: No, no. He was in a couple weeks, had come in a couple of weeks before me and he got--you had enough people in your own outfit, you know, and plus the fact we didn't have time, a lot of time for conversation. We were listening to instructions, how to set your sites, you know, and--because rifles don't shoot straight all by themselves. You got to know how to set your windage and the, well, the distance for range, and there is some skill involved in it. The guys who could do it right hit the target better than the guys who don't set it right. Some guys have eye problems and they can't shoot straight, but that's understandable. And, we had--this Lautenschlager was one--he couldn't close that one eye, you know, but--He washed out, by the way.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I was going to say, what happened to him? . . .

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Yeah, he was gone very shortly, yeah, and we had guys that didn't respect cleanliness and they didn't stick around very long, and they had a treatment for them, terrible. But, if a guy was caught not showering and so on and so forth, they had these laundry racks in every platoon area, and they were nothing but tables and running water and you take your clothes off there and you scrub them. Well, they take one of these guys that never showered, they would come out, and by instruction--the drill instructor would come out and say "Take him out and show him how to take a bath" and half a dozen guys would hold him down and they'd scrub brush--he was clean when he got done--but he never had a problem taking showers after that. I mean, they did it maybe once or twice in the whole platoon because nobody else wanted it a second time, you know, it's kind of like keel-hauling--I don't think anybody would want a second go at that (laughter).

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the rate of wash-outs then?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Geez, I really couldn't tell you. It wasn't a lot--I would say maybe--I'd say less than 10%, and I forget now, I couldn't tell you exactly how many there were in our--A platoon, I think, is 90, 90 people, and then you've got squads broken down and this and that--I've forgotten all of that stuff.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Can you give us your unit, the breakdown, division, regiment, company?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Well, the division was, really--I really don't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You don't remember the division?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Well, it was never important for us to know. We knew that we were part of--and I ended up in the Marine Air Corps--and that's an interesting thing, too, because it really upset me. When I was in boot camp--and I thought I was a pretty tough, rough kid, I wasn't mean, but I was--I liked combat and I liked to box and I liked football very much, and so I wanted--and that was really imbued was patriotism--I mean I really wanted to get after those Japs because those were bad buys and . . . While I was in boot camp, they were taking sign-ups for the Raiders--you've heard of Carlson's Raiders? And, I signed up for it, I was rejected, and I was madder than a hornet. I thought it was an affront because, hey, I was the toughest guy in the platoon, you know, we did a lot of boxing and I had boxed while I was in college and I boxed when I was a little kid, and so I could handle the gloves pretty good and I could whip these guys and they were getting into the Raiders and I'm not, you know, how come? So I went over my drill instructor's head, he didn't know, and I went to the captain who was in charge of maybe four or five platoons, I don't know how many, and I took a chance doing it, because you're not supposed to do that, that's a no-no. You got your table of organization and you got your chain of command and so on, and you do it right. Anyway, it boiled down to a very simple thing. He said the Raiders do pretty hazardous duty. They go in behind the lines, they go in when there is no support, so on and so forth, and mortality is very substantial, and your IQ is too high to serve in the Raiders as an enlisted man. Now, maybe as an officer, but I wasn't an officer, see, I had no college, because I had dropped out to join. And so, that's how then I ended up going into the Marine Air Corps. I didn't want to go into the Marine Air Corps, I wanted to go in the line company which is grunt, but they're the ones that--you know, really, the ones that I read about in that book and they were my heroes and I wanted to be one of them, but once again, they wanted the--They didn't want you to think too much if you were going to be out there and some of that activity was not considered good for your longevity, and so if you were a thinker or had the capacity to think too much, why, they thought maybe you might think twice about going up to a whatever that needed attention and getting yourself blown to bits on the way up just because somebody said, "Hey, that has to be done, you go do it," because you didn't say why, you didn't, or you didn't say (laughter) "That's a dumb thing to think--to do--" So I never got a chance to do that kind of combat. The closest that I ever got to that kind of combat was in San Diego, and there was a report of a submarine shelling the coast of California, Santa Barbara area, that never hit the newspapers, and it was kept intentionally quiet to avert--we knew about it because they broke us all out and we're guys and six weeks away from home, and all of a sudden they're issuing clowns like us live ammunition and marching us down to the beach? We're down there hoping those guys are going to show up because man, we could get an early start here, you know. They never showed, and big disappointment. But they did shell a refinery in the Goleta Beach area. And, as I say, they kept it quiet because they didn't want the citizenry to go into panic. People don't realize how close we were to losing that war. I'm telling you--it's scary. Now, I got in late, thank God. At that time I wanted to get in sooner but hindsight is better than foresight and I didn't go overseas until--I'm just trying to think--sometime in '44, maybe almost the end of '44, because I had gone from San Diego Marine Corps base to Miramar, which is an airfield outside of San Diego, and then to Santa Barbara, and I had some problems, because I didn't join the Marine Corps to be a barber, and every time they would find--my spec would catch up to me--Holy mackerel! This guy can cut hair! Like gold, you know? (laughter). And so, they would want to make me squadron barber or whatever you want to call it--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What exactly is spec?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Specifications.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Specifications?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Yeah, your specs were what your education and what your experience has been and so on and so forth, and here I am a licensed barber and wow! There aren't many of those in the Marine Corps (laughter). You should have seen some of the hair cuts! (laughter). Of course, the one they gave you in boot camp was a dandy. It takes about 60 seconds. And, I had some problems resisting it and I came close to getting in trouble because of it because I reiterated that statement many times--I didn't join the Marine Corps to cut hair. If I wanted to do that I could have got a deferment just going to a military base and getting paid to cut hair, you know. But I did it--I always had my tools with me, because I did it in the barracks if I needed money, you know. When I was in Santa Barbara, I had a good friend who shouldn't have associated with me because he was first "Louie" and I was buck private, but I don't know what our relationship, how it developed--maybe I was cutting his hair or something, I don't know--but he says "You know, you shouldn't complain." And I said "Well, why not? This is not my idea of serving my country." "Well," he says, "it may be true, it may not be true, but they say every job is just as important as the other." I said, "If that's so, how come you got bars and I got nothing?" (laughter). And, he told me, "Well," he says, "that's just the way things are." But he said, "You know, you may have a chance." "What do you mean?" "Well," he said, a new school was opening in Quantico and, as a matter of fact, it had already opened, and they're going to take four people from this base back to Quantico--this is in Santa Barbara--back to Quantico, and get trained as a navigator bombardier, and he said "Why don't you go sign up for it?" I said "There's 4,000 people on this base, they're going to take four?" (laughter). Well, I did go sign up for it, and by golly, I was one of the four, so I ended up in Quantico, and unfortunately, the school closed down because the mortality was so bad, the kind of bombing that was going on--Hell, they were losing them in training hand over fist, and when they got them into combat, it was almost 100% mortality. So, they closed the school down and took a different approach to this type of warfare. We were doing what they called "masthead and skip bombing," which means you come in (laughter) and we weren't fighting as flying Spitfires, you know, (laughter) they were slow, lumbering planes--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kind of planes did you fly?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Well, we never got to it. I never got to the point where I actually dropped a bomb from a plane or told the pilot which way to turn. (laughter). But, it was great experience, but they closed the school down and took a different approach, as I said, so I ended up back--that was my commission, see? (laughter). I didn't really mind much that I didn't have a commission because I didn't really qualify for one. So, the next thing you know I'm back in a little place in North Carolina, which was great duty because it was, I thought, great country, and this one squadron really made it nice in that respect. So--but then, back to the West Coast. Son of a guns, they told us one time we were going to pack everything up--I mean, they didn't give you much advance warning on anything--and they're building crates and packing everything in these crates and they're going to be loaded aboard a truck, I mean a boat, and they were going to go to the Riviera, the French Riviera. Wow! Of course, this was when they had already made their move and had cleared--part of that southern France was now in our hands, so it sounded good to me, you know (laughter), duty. I never had an idea that a Marine group would end up in France because I thought we were going to concentrate on the Pacific. Well, I was right! (laughter). We never got to France, ended up in the Mohave Desert, and from the Mohave Desert I went to the Marshall Islands and that was a great experience. That had been secured, I mean, we were behind all the action, and most of the airfields were. I was on a little island called Engebi. and we spent a lot of time doing nothing, because when the planes were in the air we had nothing to do, and we made necklaces and beads out of shells, you probably have seen them, and never got any--there was no hazard unless you couldn't swim and (laughter). But then we went . . . Hmm?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, specifically, what was your job, then, with the squadron?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Well, I'm not quite sure today yet. But they always managed to get me in a barber shop. Now, there were no barbershops, but the colonel came to me one time and he called me Zoot, he said, "Zoot," he said, "we're going to set you up so we have our things going." This was on Engebi, and I don't know how many squadrons there were there, but everybody had--there were four to eight people in a tent, well, not in my tent--my tent was one, just me, and it was partitioned and they were trying to take good care of me because, except for giving me stripes, they thought I was important and I always gave a good haircut. I mean, nobody--my dad's philosophy was always, don't worry about how much money you're making, you never let a customer out of your chair until you've done the best you can possibly do, and I still cut hair that way. I cut my son's hair this morning and I enjoyed doing it. That was in the basement and I don't get paid for it either (laughter). But, I have two customers, my two sons. But, I had reinforcement matting for the walls in my tent so nobody could break in--What are they going to steal for crying out loud!, but, the colonel was trying to placate me, I think, and they built me a chair that went up and down, I had hot and cold running water. The reason I had hot and cold running water is, they had a big tank setting up on a platform and had a rubber hose type thing, you know, and during the day that tropical sun--See, this was right near the equator in the Marshall Islands--and it heats that water up pretty good, and so the guys got stateside haircuts. But, I was the only one with hot and cold running water and that included the colonel (laughter). But, then I played at being a mechanic. I really wasn't that qualified because they never bothered to teach me much, I learned it on my own, and then from there, with no action there, I mean, this was probably still considered combat zone because there was a potential for bombing raids and stuff but it wasn't really. But then from there, I went to--Well, my first stop in the Marshalls was Meduro, but I don't think I had been there more than a week or so, and then they shipped us--they put us over on Engebi and then from Engebi, we went up to Iwo-shima. Now, Iwo-shima was still pretty hot, and Iwo-shima--People don't realize this--they think you're saying Iwo-jima, but it's Iwo-shima, it's a dinky little island, it rises up out of the sea, just north of Okinawa. And it was just one big airfield, I mean, and that was what was hurting Japan, so when the Japs came down to hit Okinawa, they would drop a load on us, and then on the way back they would give us what they had left over and I don't know, it wasn't in the statistics, and we didn't get official communiqués from the front office, but they said it was the heaviest bombed island in the Pacific, just for that reason, because planes would take off and they were in Japan in a matter of no time and they didn't like us being that close. And, we got them out of action there. If you were there (laughter)--. Those of us, like myself, who weren't happy because of the fact that I wasn't shooting the Japs found out that that might have been a lot easier than sitting in a place where there's shrapnel at you all the time. And, one night I woke up and there were slits in my tent. The island was secured enough that we lived in tents. At first, it was the monsoons when we hit and we lived in pup tents. You talk about misery! (laughter). I mean, you know, they teach you how to pitch your tent and you would trench around the outside of it, and we were on a little hill so the water runs off, but every time you turn over you touch that canvas and it leaks, and you don't sleep real good, and it rains 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and then just keeps on going during the monsoons. But they flew, flew every day, and the weather never slowed them down on those . . . And boy, those guys, those flyers, most of them were just kids--I mean, and they had the courage, they get in that airplane and they knew they might not come back, but it didn't seem to bother them. They were then to shoot down zeroes, you know, and Bettys and Janes and so on, so forth, and they would come back, some of the guys pretty badly shot up, and some would land, taxi a little bit, and die, right in their seat, in their cockpit, and that's tough to watch. And they were just absolutely fearless, and as I said, God, they were only out of high school for four or five years, three or fours years, whatever, you know, and they had the capacity to fly and we flew--Our squadron was Corsairs, which was the airplane as far as I was concerned, and I know nothing about airplanes. I worked on the Corsairs and almost took one off one time--I, well, we tried to keep them protected and they built these revetments, and so it would keep the bomb drops over here, then shrapnel would be diverted away from the plane. And, I am just moving one from one revetment to another and I got going a little bit too fast and the tail comes up, you know, and (laughter)--I don't know--no way it would have taken off because I had no way--because I had no training at all to fly, but it so happened the colonel saw me doing it and I heard about that one, but he was nice enough to just say "Don't do it again," and it was funny because on the inside of one of those planes, they were hideous green color on the inside, the paint on the inside of it, blue and white on the outside, but in lipstick this one gal apparently said "Take good care of this, it cost the taxpayers $80,000." Do you know what a fighter costs today? But I remember that number, $80,000. Of course, when I was making 21 bucks a month (laughter). Of course, we had no place to spend it, and--I made more than that because as this one officer said, "You make more than I do," and I said "Well," "Why don't you learn to cut hair?" (laughter).

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, what would that squadron be? Do you remember the . . . ?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: VMF 511.

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Mm Hmm, yup. Third Wing, Third Marine Wing, and part of it--you asked me for table of organization. In the Air Corps they had the wing, third wing, and then you went to MAG--Now, what the heck did MAG stand for? That was another subdivision. And then below MAG there might be six or seven squadrons in a MAG, and then I can't tell you right now what MAG meant.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Marine Air Group or something?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Yeah, something like that. That's what it would be, Marine Air Group, MAG. Why couldn't I think of that?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I just took a guess (laughter).

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: My memory! Hoo!

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, what was the highest rank that you achieved?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Uh, sergeant, yeah, yeah. We had--Well, I'm just trying to think--I think I was telling a story one time that Bill may have overheard about our going into Japan. We had--From Iwo-shima. Ernie Pyle was killed on Iwo-shima. Do you remember Ernie Pyle? Do you recognize the name? And, he was quite a -- Of course, he went through a lot of combat in Europe, and this dinky little island, he got it and it was a tough--we went in by plane. But, once we landed, we started going up this--they loaded us on these (laughter). This, ironically, is probably the closest I ever came to harm in WWII They loaded on, they call them alligators. They had wheels but they would go in the water. And, I don't how many they would hold, 60, 70 personnel, maybe more, but it was going up the side of this--the rest of the mountain so to speak--and behind it was this cliff, and down behind the cliff was about 100 feet down or more, and as we were going up this hill, hit a landmine and it blew out the brakes. The thing started going back down and we didn't realize what was happening, we were headed for that cliff, and can you believe? We ran into a stump. It was a tree that had been blown apart but it was still enough of a stump to stop us. We had a couple of guys get, you know, bones broken and so on and so forth, and all of a sudden you stop when you're rolling down a hill pretty good and your rifle is flying all over the place, you know, and we were supposed to be wearing our helmets, but some guys, you know, some guys never listen, and but that is probably as close as I ever came to any serious, serious problem. But, on Iwo-shima--and on top of that, it was raining cats and rats and it was miserable--and, but it was on Iwo-shima that we did most of our, had most of our contact with the war, I mean, actually. And, I never for one minute concerned myself with going home in one piece. I just knew I was; I was so sure, never had an ounce of fear. That's not very smart, but then again it's--Our outfit lost more guys from suicide than we did from the enemy--they just couldn't take it. I mean, night after night after night after night, no sleep, raining like the dickens, and food wasn't great (laughter), and that's a tough thing to come upon, you know, you walk into a tent and find a guy hanging from the tent pole. Just couldn't take it. And, we had one guy--I don't even want to talk about that, it was so messy--but it's funny--The guys that I respected so much were the line guys, the guys that fought Guadalcanal, Tarawa, New Guinea, God, and Hebrides, and all these exotic places, they all deserved a Congressional Medal in my book. Just being there was unbelievable. I didn't experience it, but I talked to an awful lot of guys that were, and boy, they went through hell. And, I felt the same way about the Army guys who were in the mud and the snow in northern France, right after the Bulge, you know, Battle of the Bulge, there wasn't much comfort there, either. You know, that was a bad place to hang out. And, as Brokaw says in his book, "War is a terrible way to do things," you know, and there is nothing nice about it. Back at Engebi, or Iwo-shima, we had--all of us had dug L-shaped slit trenches because in the strafing if you're underneath the level of a slit trench, people don't realize the distance when an airplane is coming in at 260 or 270 or 280 miles an hour, 300 miles an hour, that those machine gun slugs weren't hitting every three inches. I mean, they sound like they're coming so fast. Hell, there's many feet between--you know, they're going so fast that one hits here and the next one hits 15 feet down the way. So, if you were on--and we made L-shaped slit trenches--it wasn't my idea, just somebody figured it out that that's the way to do it, you want to stay alive, that's the way to do it, and you get down in that--if they're coming this way, you get in the L, that was the short, see, so only by coincidence. A plane would almost have to come down like this (gesturing) to hit you, so we were pretty safe, until one--We got pretty smart about fixing ourselves some comfort. We would get 55-gallon drums and we would split them, knock the ends of them out, split them with cold chisels and stuff. We didn't have power equipment to do that. But, we would force them open. And, these trenches would be about this wide (gesturing) and we would put that over the two ways of the trench, the L, and then we would pile dirt on top of that. It was open on the ends so you could get in and out. And there was a little ledge, you know, keep your cigarettes dry and so on, so forth, but you were in the water, I mean, if you were jumped in you knew you were going to get wet. Well, one time--and this was the middle of the night--and we had arranged candles, you know, so on and so forth, but this guy lets out a scream, and you know, you lit the candle, he's looking eye to eye with a snake. Well, it was a nice, comfortable, dry place, and he just slithered in there and made himself right at home. Well, that made it a little uncomfortable from that day forward--If you knew you were going to jump in, make sure there's no snakes in there. So what we would do, we'd throw a couple of quarts of 100 octane gasoline in there on the water, throw in a match and it-- whoosh, like that--and if any snakes were in there, either were fried or gone (laughter). We never had a problem with that again. And they tell us they were poisonous. I don't know what kind they were. In that part of the country they could very well be some kind of kinship of cobra, you know, like those brown snakes and so on. Anyway, from there to Okinawa. In Okinawa, the war was winding down then, and Okinawa was pretty good duty and it was --When I was in Okinawa they--well, I was in a movie, and things were settled down to the point where they weren't hitting us hardly at all anymore and we had just--we had beaten them, and they dropped the first bomb at Hiroshima, and then they dropped the one at Nagasaki. I think it was something like the 14th or the 16th of August, and, they announced at the movie that the Japanese were going to surrender and so on, so forth, you know (laughter). A lot of beer was drunk that night, and we had a pretty good supply of beer. Green, but it was better than nothing, and I wasn't much of a beer drinker. But, anyway, it was then that they asked for volunteers for this special squadron, if you want to call it a--it was a service detail, more than anything else--to go up into a town called Obama, I'm sorry, not Obama, Omira, Japan, that's between Sasebo, which is one of the big seaports in Kaishu and Nagasaki, which is another seaport. And, our job was to hold an airfield open for the peace planes and all of them, this and that and the other things, to get refueled and so--They were coming from the Philippines which is a fair piece away, you know, and that's where McArthur was at the time, and so we had 70 guys, and this was beautiful--We drew rations for about 450. Well, one squadron would come in, you had all these people to take care of, and typical military and government, you know, is throw more at it. And, by golly, we had things pretty good. And, the Japanese people were beautiful. Now, we were still the enemy and everything was off limits, you weren't supposed to go off base, and they catch you off base and you would be in trouble. And, I wouldn't know why a guy would go off base (laughter). It sure wasn't because the rice paddies smelled so good. But, we were 70 guys headed by a full colonel which was pretty good, too, because they took good care of him, but they told us we were the first outfit in Japan. I don't know if it's true or not. I don't even know what the dates are anymore. You think you'd never forget a thing like that but you do.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm Hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: But you got to wonder--We had supplies. Somebody was there ahead of us; it was the Navy. Boy, you talk about beautiful! That country was so beautiful! You'd come in and it seems like millions but it's hundreds, there certainly were hundreds, these small islands, and if you don't know how to get into the harbor you aren't going to get in that harbor. The pilot really had to know his stuff. You'd be in--when we went in we went by--no, we went by plane--no, we did go by--we went by boat, but our pilot--you could reach out with a 10-foot pole on either side and touch land, that's how narrow that slot was. If we had found it necessary to invade Japan to win that war, we might still be fighting it. It would have been all airborne, you know, and the casualties would have been un, unreal, so anybody, if you're counting, they did the right thing by dropping the bomb and ending that thing right now. I mean, it saved lives on both sides, but what that--I was in Nagasaki for New Years, the following New Years, I went to Nagasaki.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: In New Years '45?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: January 1, '46?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. Interesting thing, too, at least the way I understood it--All Japanese have January first as their birthday because they--when the year ends, you were born before that year ends you are a year old on the first of January. Maybe that's their easy way of keeping track of things. But anyway, I said earlier, the Japanese people, I really liked them. Remember, these were rural people for the most part and there was no military, I mean, they were gone, the hangars and the service stuff and so on, that was still there but inoperative, you know, because we had done a pretty good job on 'em. (End of Side 1, Tape 1). (Beginning of Side 2, Tape 1)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you--When you went to Nagasaki was there still any devastation there?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: I'm sorry?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you went to Nagasaki, was there any devastation left?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Oh, it was flattened. I mean, and the irony--I mean it was just nothing there, just blew it all down. There was one wall, and it was really funny and I can close my eyes and see it today, it was a brick wall still standing and a closed green door. That door was there, and it was closed, and it was all intact. I saw it from the road but I didn't go up to test it or anything. But it must have been that the force came the length of the wall, not the breadth of it, because nothing--and it was a peanut compared to what they have now, the bomb they dropped, and I don't think that the damage in Nagasaki was as severe as it was in Hiroshima, and why that would be, I don't know. I was under the impression they were the same, same, same . . .

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Kinds of atom bombs . . .

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Yeah, they're--Well, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, well, one was Fat Man, one was Little Boy--I mean it was two different kinds of reactions. I think the devastation . . .

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Well, maybe one was detonated in the air and the other one was closer to the, you know, okay . . . And it was pretty nasty. I saw some, saw some people who had been badly burned and it looked like their skin was just melted on them, you know. They had survived, and they seemed to be doing what people do, although it is very likely that a lot of them succumbed to radiation poisoning a year, two years later, you know, three years later, I don't know. It was pretty nasty stuff, but--I loved Japan, and we . . .

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you talk much to any of the people over in Nagasaki when you were there?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. We had a hotel room, and we usually went in groups. They told us it is not smart to go, you know, by yourself anywhere, but we went to more than--I only went to Nagasaki the one time and that was more of a curiosity trip than anything else, and I spent most of time going and coming. I had my own jeep. Not that I was important, but everybody had their own jeep (laughter). We were so over-supplied it was ridiculous---

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (Laughter).

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: --and nobody worked two days in a row, I mean, you were 24 on, 24 off, and, like firemen, you know, of that 24, you were sleeping 16 of it (laughter). And--or doing something--and we, we would get in our jeeps, you know, and we would take off for this little town called Obama, right on the seashore, somewhere I've got a folder showing this hotel and everything, really fabulous! Oh, God, it was gorgeous! And, we would, we would go up there, and the irony of the whole thing, and this is typical of young men, we spent more time playing Monopoly, when there is all this fresh, new stuff to go out and absorb and what did we do? I did the same thing when I had liberty, go into town, sit in a room and play cards, and--but that's young men for you, and I played a lot of cards. This hotel was beautiful and we ate there and the food was strictly Japanese, and don't ask for a piece of meat because they didn't serve meat, and I learned to eat fish, you know, and these delicacies--the cheek, the little muscle in the cheek of the fish--Oh, that's so good! And, I ate octopus and I had no problem with it. I had one really funny experience while at this hotel. We had a lot of funny experiences, because you're bound to have funny experiences when you're so out of place, you know. Excuse me. This hotel had a--and this was in the --this--Obama existed because they had multitudes of sulfur, hot sulfur springs, and people would come into the hotel and in the basement of the hotel they had this great big pool, and we went down and decided we are going to take one of these baths, you know, and we were warned. And, incidentally, the local families would come in and they would take off their clothes and they would climb into the pool and they would think nothing of it. Of course, we were wearing our skivvies, our modesty. But they said, "Don't stay in more than 20 to 25 minutes, you'll be sorry if you do." And, we had this one guy and his name was Shimkes (sp) and I can't think of his first name, built like a Greek God, you know, a weightlifter and so on, and we all lifted weights--we found gears and rods and reinforcement rods--we made up our own weights and it was something to do. But this guy, before the Marines was a weightlifter, strong as a bull, and built beautifully. Well, nobody was going to tell Shimkes to get out of that pool in 20 minutes; he stayed an extra 15-20 minutes, and he come out, he's toweling himself off, you know, and Oh--He hit the ground before the towel did. He went out like a light. Just sapped you of energy. I guess it's good for you, but not too much of it. And that was a pretty funny situation, but the really funniest thing was, we were playing Monopoly one time, and I love Monopoly, I love any kind of game, I like to be competitive, but this one day we were playing Monopoly and we were sitting on these straw mats, you know, beautiful, room, really, it's like out of a movie! At least we took time to look around to that extent, you know, and we--I remember I got a haircut from a lady barber--first time in my life--I didn't know that ladies could cut hair! Why not, you know, but we were going back to the room to get--play Monopoly and one of the guys bought some incense. Now, incense is a big thing in Japan, and we had this thing in the middle of the room which contained charcoal and, you know, it was lit all the time because it was fairly cool as I recall at that time, not too far from late fall or early spring. And, we're sitting there playing Monopoly and our incense is burning away on the charcoal, you know, and so on, so forth, and all of a sudden all hell breaks loose! People running up and down the halls, and yelling and so on and so forth. Turns out, that incense that this guy had bought, and we didn't know incense from incense, (laughter) was the incense you burn when somebody died in the house!

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (Laughter).

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: So they're looking for the body! (laughter) Running up and down the halls, and I mean, the Japanese recognize these various scents, and we didn't know what was going on until finally someone explained it to us, and they were able to determine that the smell was coming from our room. I thought that was pretty funny, and---But the people were so gracious! I had--One of my duties was to, not maintain because I had a work crew to do the work, but I ran a, I guess what they called a commissary, and I had the only key to the cooler, with tons and tons of sugar, and boy, I was getting nailed every day, somebody wanted to--This one captain tried to get me to make sugar available and he flew to China three times a week. He said we would each pick up a couple grand on each trip because sugar is selling for four bucks a pound and we had tons of it! Tea, coffee, sugar, beans, you name it, we had it. And I had beef in the reefer, butter, I mean, these privates got fed pretty good when they came in and their staff, you know, but we ate the same thing. And, but I was being approached constantly--"Come on"--but I did give away some sugar. I'd give it to, see these little old ladies and kids, they would be out on the reef, and when the tide would go out everything is out at the edge of the water, and they would be picking up these little shells, the mollusks, they weren't any bigger than a dime, maybe, but there was meat in 'em, and of course, they were such patient people. And, they would spend a whole day getting a little cup-full, and I felt sorry for them and I would call somebody over and had to be very careful because I didn't know what kind of trouble I was going to get myself into, and I would give them a little 5-lb bag of sugar. Boy, you'd have thought I'd have given them a diamond ring, they were so grateful for it. But I had to stop doing that because--exactly what--if I had thought about it I wouldn't have done it because the next day there were six times as many people out there collecting seashells and so I had to say --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Laughter.

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: --whatever little Japanese I knew, "No way." But WWII for me was just for the most part one great experience after another. As I said, I never worried about, about getting hurt . . . Technically, (laughter) I got hit in the leg one time on the way to that slit trench and I didn't know it until everything was all over and I got out and my pants were all wet. I mean, they were wet from being in the water, but it was red wet (laughter). And, it was little tiny pieces. It wasn't a very big mark, and it apparently penetrated and it might still be in there for all I knew, but it has never given me any trouble, and I never told anybody about it because --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Shrapnel?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Well, yeah, something, who knows? It was--Obviously, it was sharp enough to break the skin and go on in. It bled pretty good but never had any consequences so I never said diddly about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That came during an air raid?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, technically, you must have been eligible for a Purple Heart?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Well, you could get a Purple Heart for almost anything--you hit yourself in the thumb with a hammer you . . .

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (Laughter).

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: (Laughter). Well, we had guys put in for a Purple Heart, you can't believe! They wanted a medal, you know! But we got enough.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm Hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: I mean, we got enough for just being there, you know, you got your oak leaf clusters and all that--I don't even know what they meant, and I don't know . . . I made the mistake of letting my one son take my Marine Corps Blues for a Halloween party one time and that was the end of it, I never saw it again.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I heard this story at least once before when somebody let (inaudible) take medals (inaudible)--

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Yeah, it had to--you know had the ribbons, you know--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Laugher

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: --and my sharpshooter medal and whatever it was, and--I'm not--I've still get enough trinkets, I've got some emblems and belts and I must have four or five Japanese rifles and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Oh, yes. A Samurai sword, and--someday I will probably take them to one of these shows and sell 'em because they don't mean anything to anybody unless it is a collector.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you mean in Japan, or--

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Well, some of them my brother brought home. He was an ensign in the Navy, but that's a story I got to tell you, too, this is another funny story. Most of my stories are funny! (Laughter) And I'm happy to say that. He had a certain amount he could ship home. Enlisted men didn't have that privilege, but I did get a couple home and--a sword and a bayonet, so and so--I got two--I still use 'em too, machetes! As a matter of fact, I just oiled one the other day, it got some rust on it. And the funny thing is, one of 'em was made in my home town, Geneva at the (name of foundry?)______________.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And that, the Japanese army had it?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: No, no, no. It was one of ours. Yeah we used mach--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, one of ours, oh.

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: I have a jungle knife that I carry in my van all the time. It's got a blade about that thick (gesturing) and about that long. It weighs a ton. And, I don't ever want to get hit with that sucker.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Inaudible.

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Well, it was used for whacking bamboo down, and so on and so forth in those jungles. Now, we didn't need it because we never had that problem and, but the line company guys many times would get into the jungle, the jungles were terrible, and those poor guys had to, you know, crawl through the slime and the--I was never in a marsh in my, you know, in the military, never had to go through water up to my chin, holding, you know, everything you own up over your head, and because God knows what you're going to bump into in those jungle marshes and swamps. But, they did it, and they would come--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You talked about some of the pilots that were lost. Did you lose any friends?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, you didn't know them that well, then?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Well, the pilots, no, because once again, the pilots, they were a group of their own. I knew 'em better than most guys did because I had barber tools and that leads me to a story, then I better shut up.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Laughter.

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: But, relative to Jim, he was a--I was on Iwo-shima and a lot of short tempers in those days, like when you don't get any sleep for three or four days in a row, you get exhaustion type sleep, you know, but I got a letter from Jim, he's an ensign now, I'm still the lowest--I may have been a corporal at the time, no more than that. And, it's the only letter he ever wrote me all during the time that we were in the service, and he was in Boca Chica, Florida. He was a gunnery officer in the Navy. He was an ensign and he had finished up--I think he went to Notre Dame, went to Oberland, then to Notre Dame and to Great Lakes and so on, so forth, and they ended up in Boca Chica, and he's relating this story about, "Oh, we've got an enlisted man who keeps our beer cold and baits our hook . . ." Well, being an enlisted man and being short of sleep, I didn't take to that too well, so I wrote him a scathing letter, I mean, it wasn't very nice, but I didn't like what--you know, he putting me down as an enlisted man, and it irritated me. Next day, two days later, Col Pugh calls me into his tent--he didn't call me, he sent somebody to get me--because we want to talk to him (sic). Well, you don't waste any time when a colonel wants to talk to you--and he's all over me about this letter I wrote to my brother, and he says, "You can't talk that way to an officer." I said, "He's no officer, he's my brother." (Laughter) He said, "You gotta rewrite it." I said, "Why don't you tear it up?" He said, "You don't want to send it," and I said "No, and I'm not gonna rewrite it," and he says, "Okay." He says, "When can I get a haircut?" (Laughter).

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (Laughter). Do you remember anything else about letters, any memories of the letters from home or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Well, a lot of letters got lost. And mail call was important. Pictures I got from girlfriends that somehow got pictures over there, and they were always welcome. My sister would write and my parents would write. My dad never wrote because he was old country Italian and he couldn't write in English very well, and I, like most kids, when he wanted to teach me Italian I was too busy, you know, and when my mother wanted to teach me German I was too busy, so everything had to be English. But, the letters--the letters will pick you up like almost nothing else, I mean, no telephone calls, you know, and no tapes, and . . . And, I talked to guys who were in Vietnam and they got tapes from family and they say, "Boy, you can't believe, priceless!" Listen to 'em until there was no oxide left on the tape, you know. People, people at home just don't know, there's no way for them to know, and I think for the most part the guys don't complain an awful lot because it makes the folks at home feel bad. You know, if I had--My mother was a mother hen. She had been a nurse and she just, her kids boy! She took good care of us. And, even though she was tough, she would have been--she would have felt bad, you know, if somebody wasn't feeding me right or if I complained about the food. I never complained about the food. As a matter of fact, I ate pretty good. I weighed 230-some pounds--and I'm 200 now, But, I let it be known to the chief chefs, the heads of the mess hall that I was interested in playing poker with them and eating at their table and I could cut hair and I, Hey, I did that, I took advantage when, you know, they're going to make me cut hair, by God, I am going to get what I could out of it, so, and I rarely drew money off the books because I didn't have to, I needed some money, I would put up a GI Can--you know what a GI Can is, don't you? Rubbish and garbage can? Set it up in the head, and the head is the latrine. Marines used Navy language--A ladder--stairs are ladders, and walls are bulkheads and so on and so on and so on. But, if I needed some money, no problem, you know, but I ate with the cooks, I played cards with 'em and that meant that I didn't get in line for food and I didn't--And we ate pretty good, not like the Navy. No, when I was--I found out what the Navy was like when I was in Okinawa-- After I had been to Japan my tour of duty was up and I was supposed to go home and so on, so forth, and--Well, this leads to a story that you won't believe. Isn't it funny how one story comes out of another?--Just like a bunch of guys telling jokes--all of a sudden-- (laughter)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Inaudible.

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: The--oh, boy--I talked about eating with the cooks and so on, so forth, and, Oh--When we were--when we had come back from Japan, we flew down into Okinawa and the--oh boy--my memory's bad--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were talking about that (inaudible) Navy? What the Navy didn't get --

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Well, what happened--This was--We had nothing to do. It was the most boring thing, because it was really, waiting to get on board ship and go home, and I think they were going to fly us home. And, we had to wait for an AKA. Incidentally, I love to play chess and I learned during this time. I bumped into a guy from my home town, and he was a parachute packer, and his name was Bill Pouche (sp) and we went--When I bumped into him we were going to sit down and talk and he says, "Do you play chess?" and I says "No." "Oh," he says, "great game." And he taught me how to play chess. And I have been playing ever since. But we got aboard--finally, finally, we got aboard this APA AKA, holds about 2000, and thank God for chess because we were on that stupid boat for 30 days, in the harbor! Now, what do you think a couple thousand Marines come up with as far as why are we sitting here? I mean, it was terrible. And one of the most common bits of scuttlebutt--scuttlebutt, rumors, was that we were going to hit the Russians from the east and we're going to stay and do some more, you know. Never heard one guy say, "Oh, I want to go home." Of course, we all wanted to go home, but nobody--and almost like it was orchestrated--better we do it now than our kids have to do it 50 years from now, and it wasn't true, but we sat in that stupid boat for 30 days. Now, weather was nice for the most part, so we sat up on deck most of the time because being below decks--no good, bad news! A bunk was about that wide (gesturing), you know, and if you turned over you'd bump into the bump--the bunk--easy for you to say--(laughter)--bump into the bunk on top of you, and that usually got a response of some kind.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything else about what you did for entertainment? Do you remember USO shows or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Never had a USO show--U-S-O show, show up. I'm having a tough time. We did have movies. Especially toward the end. During most of the time we didn't. Of course, movies are outdoors, and show a lot of light and one thing we didn't want to do was for a lot of light around, you know, so there weren't any movies until we got into Okinawa in the waning days, and I think the movie that I was watching had Ella Raines in it when they announced, when the movie was shut off, and we thought, there goes the film again, you know, the projector broke or whatever--that happened frequently, but they stopped it to make the announcement and never started it again because nobody was really interested in the movie anymore, but Ella Raines was in it, and I thought she was great. Do you remember Ella Raines:

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So did they make the announcement? What announcement was it?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: That they dropped a bomb.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, that they dropped a bomb.

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: And, that they expected the Japanese to sue for peace (sic) and it turns out to be true.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything about the day FDR died? Any specific memories about the day FDR died? Roosevelt?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Oh, oh, oh, oh, oh, oh. I remember, I remember the day and getting the news and so on and so forth, but most of the guys didn't react to it, and I think one reason for it: There were a lot of rumors around about, well, FDR knew that the Japanese were going to hit Pearl Harbor and everybody had friends that were lost in Pearl Harbor and we had all been to Pearl Harbor and we didn't like what we saw. And that, whether it was true or not, and subsequently, I guess there was a pretty good understanding that he knew or expected the Japanese to strike, and that he kind of wanted an excuse for getting into the war, and that was beautiful, perfect--you know, a day of infamy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Backtracking a bit, do you remember the day Pearl Harbor was bombed?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Oh, yes. Oh, yeah. Yeah, I couldn't believe it. I was in high school and absolutely no way could that happen, and people don't realize how ill equipped we were, how lucky we were, for things like the Badler-Midway. That was so close to being a non-victory and it could have very well put Japanese on the West Coast. I mean, they had us. We were so poorly equipped. And, not everything was heroics and glory and patriotism and so on, so forth. And my own personal feeling about FDR is not the way you are supposed to think about your Commander in Chief. Of course, I have always been apolitical--I'm not real fond of politicians--not--individually, I have known a lot of them and they're beautiful people, but when they're playing top politicians it's a different game and never, never appreciated it, but for the most part, the guys didn't, didn't respond to it negatively because I think the majority of people resented him, and we all did not like Eleanor. I don't know of anybody who liked--Well, Eleanor, Eleanor had, what would you call it? Because she wasn't a dummy, she was an educated gal and many people claimed she was the power behind the chair in the White House, that had a better head than FDR, although FDR had some brilliant social concepts. She came overseas and was talking to a group of Marines in Guam or someplace like that where there was a big contingent and she made the statement that she's going to recommend that when the war is over that all Marines have to go to a rehabilitation program so they'll know how to behave when they're back on the streets, that the girls wouldn't be safe when the Marines got home. Well, that was some truth! (laughter). No, that's not true. I saw Marines do dumb things when they had a snootful of alcohol, I saw Navy guys do it, and I saw Army guys do it, and I saw civilians do it, so what's the big deal?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: But she for some reason, whether she was being funny--Boy, you talk about--they got her out of there in a hurry. I mean, they were afraid of a riot, because she--how could--? Well, she did, and so that didn't help FDR and when he died, so what? Big deal! And who's this Truman guy? Nobody knew who Truman was. Little did we know that he was going to stop the war for us. Tom, I know I've waxed long and--get me started and I enjoy talking about those days, and believe me when I say it: One of the best things that ever happened to me was to be taken into the Marines, and I don't know what I'd have done if they wouldn't have taken me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Is there any one vivid memory that comes to mind when you think back to that time?

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: No, I, I, I don't think so. See, there was never--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It was a collage (laughter)--

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Yeah, it was never a case of any real impact. The only, the only time I ever fired a rifle in anger was when we were on Iwo-shima and at night these guys--Believe me, those things were all just honeycombed with caves and the island was secure but they weren't all gone. Plus the fact, they could come across from Okinawa when the tide was down. And they would be up on top of this big hill, and they'd be shooting down into our compound! And, so we would sit out there and we would see a muzzle flash, we would shoot at the muzzle. That's all you could do, you didn't see anybody. And we had an experience one time on a, sort of a boredom patrol. A small group of guys decided they were going to go out and have some adventure, and went into this one cave and out comes, out comes from the back of the cave, I don't know, two, three, four, and--but they weren't soldiers, they weren't military, but they had the sword up and they were going--they started to swing, and the only guy that had a side arm was this one fella who had no business having it, everybody else had an M1, M1 is a big piece, and it is not easy--You don't take one of those things in the small confines of a cave and start shooting because it ricochets off--But anyway, to make a long story short, the only guy with a, with a hand gun, a 45, didn't know how to get the safety off it. Now, the irony of this story is that that would get your attention when all of a sudden the only guy who can do you any good can't do you any good and somehow or another we were able to get out there without any, any--no damage, no damage at all and we didn't even have to kill these people. They were natives, but they were scared stiff! They knew what was coming off. We thought they were there to kill 'em (sic). And they found this big, long sword and that's the only weapon they had. It whacked--this guy put his rifle up, you know, and they just cut that stacking swivel right off it, Boy, I tell you . . . But, fortunately, nothing came out of it. But, this kid, and I can't think of his name now--I didn't think I'd ever forget it, but I can't think of it, and he was sort of a--He really didn't belong in the Corps, and I guess this is why he had latched onto that 45. How he got it, nobody knows, because it wasn't issued to him, and--but it made him feel big--and we had--After the war was over and they were letting guys go home that had been over--we, we had guys in our outfit who had been overseas since January or February of 1942, I mean, a month, two, three months after the war started! And, this one fella's name was Craven (sp), was waiting for the truck to come along and pick him up to take him to the airplane. And this was on Okinawa. And this, this guy came in--I want to call him Sam but it's not Sam--Anyway, he came in and got that 40--pulls his 45 out, you know, and just flopping it around and he said "I'm gonna put it right between your eyes." Damn thing went off, hit this guy--he hadn't been home since early 1942, and he'd already written his parents that he'd be home for Christmas or whatever, you know, and-- killed him instantly. And that was perhaps--we all cried over that one. It was probably the worst thing that happened all the time I was in the Corps and it was stupid! I mean, here was this guy--there wasn't an ounce of intent there--and they, they didn't do anything except put him on sort of a probationary status until he got back to the states and then discharged him. Never filed . . . You know, that was one of those things . . .

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm Hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Shouldn't have done it, didn't mean to do it, but he did it, and Craven, you know, after serving through an awful lot--He had been at Okinawa and had been at Guadalcanal and several of the real hot spots, but most of the guys wanted, wanted to win the war in the worst way and they wanted to do all they could to help--didn't--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm Hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert Zito
sp.p: Really, didn't hear the grousing that a lot of people talk about. And, I've talked to Army friends and Navy friends and they're all pretty much the same. It was a great generation!
[Conclusion of Interview]
